title: A Partner Has Taxable Profit but No Matching Cash Distribution
summary: Build a tax reserve around the K-1 forecast rather than the cash that reaches the partner’s bank account.
situation: A minority business owner expects another profitable year, but the partnership is retaining cash. Household spending depends on irregular distributions. The owner asks whether moving the interest into another entity would make the tax bill follow the cash received. A second concern is a possible refinancing distribution, which feels like profit even though it comes from borrowing.
decision: The immediate planning problem is liquidity. A complicated ownership change would not answer how the household will fund an approaching payment. The analysis needs three separate columns: allocated taxable income, distributions actually received, and the partner’s outside tax basis. Combining those columns makes a cash shortage look like an accounting error.
rule: Partners generally report their allocated partnership income even when the partnership retains the money. A cash distribution and an allocation of profit are separate events; distribution tax treatment also requires a basis review.
recommendation: Request a current-year K-1 forecast and distribution schedule, then prepare a household tax projection. Ask the partnership to explain its tax-distribution policy and expected timing. Reserve cash for the projected shortfall before committing to another investment. Review debt allocations and outside basis before describing a refinancing distribution as tax-free.
records: Current and prior K-1s plus the partnership agreement
Capital contributions, distribution history and outside-basis workpapers
Debt schedules and the partnership’s current profit forecast
alternative: If the partnership cannot release cash, the recommendation becomes a funding and payment plan rather than an entity redesign. If a sale or ownership transfer is already planned, model that transaction separately before changing ownership. A lender balance or capital-account figure alone is not a substitute for outside basis.
deliverable: A calendar of expected allocations, distributions and tax payments, with a documented funding gap. This case does not claim that the partnership made a distribution or that a tax balance was eliminated.

title: A Law Firm Partner Reviews Guaranteed Payments Before Forming an LLC
summary: Separate guaranteed payments, profit allocations and distributions before recommending a new entity.
situation: A professional-services partner receives both guaranteed payments and a share of firm profits. Income has risen, and the partner wants to know whether an LLC could reduce the tax cost. A spouse also works for the firm, so household wages, partnership income and benefit opportunities overlap.
decision: The first question is what the partner actually owns and how the firm pays for services. An LLC is a legal structure, and its name alone does not establish a different federal income-tax result. The firm’s agreement, professional ownership rules and existing compensation arrangements constrain what can change.
rule: Guaranteed payments are determined without regard to partnership income. Their reporting is distinct from distributions and from the partner’s distributive share. Each component needs to be identified before evaluating employment-tax treatment.
recommendation: Reconcile the K-1 to the partnership agreement and payment ledger. Ask the firm’s tax team which changes are permitted, then compare the existing arrangement with any legally available alternative. Coordinate the household projection with the firm’s retirement-plan administrator rather than assuming that a new personal entity creates a separate contribution opportunity.
records: Partnership agreement and recent K-1s
Guaranteed-payment detail and cash distribution ledger
Spouse’s W-2 and all firm retirement-plan documents
alternative: When the firm will not permit an ownership change, improve estimated payments, benefit coordination and recordkeeping within the current structure. If the partner has a genuinely separate consulting activity, analyze that business on its own facts. Do not relabel law-firm earnings as another company’s revenue without a supportable legal and tax basis.
deliverable: An income map that identifies who earns each payment, how it is reported, and which planning decisions require firm approval. The recommendation is a review sequence, not a promise that an LLC lowers the bill.

title: A Tenant Leaves Late in the Year: Convert to an STR Now or Wait?
summary: Test operational readiness and participation before rushing a long-term rental conversion for a deduction.
situation: A salaried household owns a long-term rental whose tenant plans to leave late in the year. The owners are considering short-term stays and a cost segregation study. The remaining weeks must accommodate repairs, furnishing, local approvals, photography and guest bookings while both owners continue their regular work.
decision: A year-end target can compress several separate decisions into one. Buying furniture does not establish that the property is ready for guests. A reservation forecast does not establish the actual average stay. A proposed task calendar does not prove that the owners performed the work. The business should be operationally credible before a tax projection assumes a new activity profile.
rule: An average customer-use period of seven days or less can remove an activity from the rental-activity category under the passive rules. Material participation remains a separate test; short stays alone do not establish a nonpassive loss.
recommendation: Build a readiness checklist with an owner for every task and a realistic launch date. Confirm local operating requirements. Track owner and vendor work as it occurs, retain reservation records, and have the preparer analyze the transition year. Order the study after the basis and intended reporting approach are understood, not as a substitute for those decisions.
records: Tenant move-out and renovation completion records
Permit, listing, guest-stay and availability records
Contemporaneous owner task logs and vendor work details
alternative: If the property cannot operate properly before year-end, a deliberate launch in the following year may protect cash and produce better records. Compare both years before accelerating expenses. Do not manufacture stays, hours or an availability date to support the preferred answer.
deliverable: A go-or-wait decision with a launch checklist and two-year projection. The case describes a recommendation, not proof that a conversion qualified or that wages were offset.
source_label: IRS Publication 925: Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules

title: A Former Home Becomes a Rental in Stages
summary: Reconstruct the conversion timeline and business-use allocation before calculating depreciation.
situation: An owner first rents one portion of a home while living in the rest, then moves out and makes the entire property available to tenants. Renovations occur between those dates. A proposed cost segregation calculation uses the current market value of the whole property, which may not match the depreciation basis or the amount used for rental purposes during each period.
decision: There is no single conversion date for every dollar in this fact pattern. The occupied portion, first rental area, later improvements and furnishings may follow different timelines. The planning work starts with a property history rather than a target deduction. It also needs to preserve information for a future sale.
rule: For a personal residence converted to rental use, depreciation basis generally starts with the lower of adjusted basis or fair market value at conversion. Land is not depreciable, and personal and rental use must be separated.
recommendation: Create a dated floor plan and use schedule. Reconcile the original closing statement, capital improvements and conversion-date valuation. Allocate land and the rental portion using supportable records, then establish asset schedules for each applicable service date. Have the preparer review personal-use days and the eventual sale implications before projecting a benefit.
records: Purchase closing statement and improvement invoices
Conversion-date valuation and land allocation support
Floor plans, leases, move-out dates and personal-use calendar
alternative: If conversion value is below adjusted cost, an appreciation-based calculation will overstate depreciation. If only one unit is rented, a whole-building deduction is inappropriate. A future move back into the property would require another review rather than simply continuing the same business-use assumptions.
deliverable: A conversion workpaper linking each asset to its basis, rental percentage and service date. No deduction amount is claimed in this illustrative case because those records determine the answer.

title: Cost Segregation After a 1031 Exchange Starts With the Exchange Basis
summary: Keep carryover basis, excess basis and separately purchased furnishings distinct on a replacement rental.
situation: A rental investor replaces a long-held property through a 1031 exchange and plans to operate the replacement as a short-term rental. The owner asks for a cost segregation estimate based on the new contract price, including furniture acquired around closing. The prior property’s accumulated depreciation has not yet been supplied to the study team.
decision: The engineer and return preparer need the same starting numbers. A new purchase agreement does not erase the old property’s depreciation history. Before deciding which components may receive accelerated treatment, the team must explain how the exchange moved basis into the replacement asset and which costs represent additional investment.
rule: Like-kind exchange property generally requires separate consideration of carryover and excess basis for depreciation. The replacement property’s market price is not automatically an entirely new depreciable basis. Special elections and asset-level facts can affect the calculation.
recommendation: Have the preparer complete an exchange-basis bridge before finalizing the study. Give the engineer the prior depreciation schedule, exchange workpapers and replacement closing statement. Identify furnishings purchased separately and avoid counting them again inside a building allocation. Reconcile the final engineering schedule to the return’s fixed-asset ledger.
records: Form 8824 and qualified-intermediary closing package
Relinquished-property adjusted basis and depreciation detail
Replacement settlement statement, allocation support and furnishing invoices
alternative: If exchange reporting is incomplete, commission a preliminary scope review rather than a final savings claim. If the replacement property has mixed personal use or an uncertain operating plan, resolve those questions alongside basis. A sound study can still be useful, but its tax value depends on the return treatment and the investor’s ability to use resulting deductions.
deliverable: An agreed basis bridge and a study-to-return reconciliation. This case makes no claim that the full purchase price qualifies for accelerated depreciation or that an exchange creates a guaranteed wage offset.
source_label: IRS Publication 946: How To Depreciate Property

title: An S-Corp Election Is in Place, but Owner Payroll Is Missing
summary: Confirm the election and address compensation reporting before treating owner draws as a tax strategy.
situation: A business owner believes an S election was filed, takes regular draws and has not run owner payroll. The household also earns wages from an unrelated employer. The owner asks whether the outside W-2 means the business can distribute all remaining earnings without wages.
decision: Two issues need separate answers: whether the IRS accepted the election and how the owner’s services were compensated. Filing an election is not a payroll process. A bank transfer labeled distribution does not establish its correct treatment, and an outside employer does not document the work performed for this company.
rule: An S corporation must pay reasonable compensation for shareholder services before treating relevant payments as non-wage distributions. The amount depends on the services and facts; a fixed salary-to-distribution percentage is not a universal rule.
recommendation: Obtain the election acceptance and reconcile owner transfers. Document duties, hours and compensation evidence with a qualified payroll adviser. Determine the appropriate correction process for affected periods, then establish regular payroll, withholding and a year-end review. Compare total household taxes only after the company’s reporting obligations are understood.
records: Election filing and IRS acceptance
Owner draw ledger, payroll reports and filed entity returns
Job duties, time commitments and comparable compensation support
alternative: If the election was never effective, use the actual tax classification and evaluate available relief rather than assuming S-corp treatment. If draws include loan repayments or reimbursements, substantiate those items separately. Corrections may require coordinated payroll and income-tax filings; simply relabeling the general ledger is insufficient.
deliverable: A documented classification, compensation analysis and correction checklist with clear responsibility for each filing. No payroll-tax savings amount is asserted because the missing facts drive both compliance and the comparison.

title: A Growing Practice Evaluates Retirement Funding With Employees in the Picture
summary: Compare owner benefits with employee funding and recurring commitments before adding a pension design.
situation: A practice owner has a strong profit year and already contributes to an existing retirement plan. The practice employs clinical and administrative staff, and the owner is interested in a cash balance or other defined benefit arrangement. A large current deduction sounds appealing, but future collections and staffing costs remain uncertain.
decision: The useful comparison is not the largest possible owner contribution. It is the household benefit after employee costs, administration and funding commitments, while preserving enough operating cash. Related businesses and a spouse’s employment can also change the information the plan specialist needs.
rule: Retirement plan design must account for eligible employees and applicable coverage rules. Defined benefit plans involve actuarial calculations and funding obligations; an owner-only contribution estimate is not a complete plan proposal.
recommendation: Obtain a full employee census and ownership map before requesting illustrations. Ask a third-party administrator and actuary to compare the current plan with realistic alternatives over several years. Put employee costs, fees and contribution flexibility beside the owner’s projected benefit. Stress-test a lower-profit year before making a recurring commitment.
records: Employee census with compensation, age and service dates
Existing plan documents and contribution history
Ownership information for related entities and a multi-year cash forecast
alternative: When profits are volatile or expansion needs cash, improving the existing plan may be more practical than adding another obligation. When recurring surplus and staffing patterns support a larger design, obtain a formal proposal with deadlines and administration responsibilities. Age alone does not answer whether a particular plan is suitable.
deliverable: A side-by-side funding comparison and a sustainable contribution budget. This case does not claim a plan was adopted, a contribution limit was approved or a deduction was secured.

title: A Couple Separates a Syndication’s Tax Illustration From Its Investment Merits
summary: Translate a sponsor’s depreciation illustration into an investor-specific decision before committing capital.
situation: A high-income household receives a rental syndication proposal featuring a large first-year depreciation number. The presentation also shows distributions and projected appreciation. The couple wants an independent view because the person introducing the investment may receive compensation if they proceed.
decision: A deal-level deduction is not the same as this household’s current tax savings. The couple also needs to distinguish cash yield, return of capital, an annualized marketing figure and the return over the full holding period. A favorable tax illustration cannot resolve weak operating assumptions or limited access to invested cash.
rule: Passive losses can be limited even when a partnership allocates depreciation to an investor. The taxpayer’s participation, other passive income and applicable loss limitations matter; a K-1 deduction does not automatically offset wages.
recommendation: Have an adviser independent of the sale review the investor-specific tax assumptions. Request a fee schedule, distribution waterfall, debt terms and downside cash-flow model. Ask who receives compensation and whether the presentation assumes immediate use of every deduction. Evaluate the investment without the proposed tax benefit, then add only the benefit the preparer can support.
records: Offering memorandum, subscription documents and fee disclosures
Projected K-1 assumptions and depreciation support
Household passive-loss carryforwards and current-year income projection
alternative: If losses are expected to be suspended, treat that as a timing difference in the decision model rather than immediate spending money. If fees or downside assumptions remain unclear, delaying the investment is a valid recommendation. An independent review does not guarantee investment performance or validate a sponsor’s claims.
deliverable: A decision memo separating investment economics, liquidity, conflicts and usable tax benefits. The scenario identifies no sponsor and makes no allegation about a particular firm or adviser.

title: A Rental Refinance Funds Renovations: Which Costs Enter the Asset Schedule?
summary: Trace loan proceeds and actual project costs instead of adding the refinancing balance to depreciation basis.
situation: A rental owner refinances a small multifamily property and uses part of the proceeds for renovations. Other proceeds remain in cash or pay different obligations. The owner wants a cost segregation study and assumes the full new loan balance increases the building’s depreciable cost.
decision: The project needs a source-and-use reconciliation. The lender’s balance describes financing, while invoices describe what was acquired or improved. Replacing an old loan, holding cash and constructing an improvement are different uses of proceeds, even when they appear in one settlement package.
rule: Capital improvements can increase adjusted basis. Borrowing itself does not create an additional building asset. Loan costs, repairs and capital improvements require their own classification rather than one combined renovation total.
recommendation: Reconcile the refinance closing statement to bank activity and vendor payments. Group project costs by work performed, completion date and property component. Have the preparer distinguish repairs from capital additions and review how interest follows the use of proceeds. Give the study team supported asset costs rather than the amount borrowed.
records: Original and refinance settlement statements
Loan-proceeds ledger, bank statements and contractor invoices
Prior depreciation schedule and project completion records
alternative: If invoices are missing, reconstruct them before estimating a deduction. If a portion of the property remains personal, allocate costs appropriately. If proceeds funded a separate business or personal purchase, keep that use visible instead of attributing it to rental improvements.
deliverable: A project ledger tying financing to expenditures and expenditures to the tax asset schedule. This case does not assume that all renovation spending is immediately deductible or that the new mortgage balance is depreciable.

title: A Physician Puts Overdue Returns Ahead of a New Tax Structure
summary: Establish filing status, reconstruct records and quantify balances before adding another entity or investment.
situation: A physician has moved between employment and independent contracting. Several personal and business returns may be missing or incorrect, and business and personal spending have partly mixed. The physician wants a forward-looking tax plan but does not yet have a reliable picture of prior balances or current estimated payments.
decision: A sophisticated new strategy would rest on an uncertain baseline. The adviser first needs to distinguish an unfiled return from a filed return requiring correction, identify the actual entity classification for each year, and determine which notices carry deadlines. The current year still needs attention while that cleanup proceeds.
rule: Past-due returns remain filing obligations even when the taxpayer cannot pay the entire balance. IRS records and notices help identify the periods involved, but a substitute return does not replace a taxpayer’s opportunity to file a complete return with supported deductions.
recommendation: Create a year-by-year filing matrix and obtain appropriate transcripts and prior returns. Reconstruct the books, reconcile contractor income and payroll, and assign each missing filing to a preparer. Address notice deadlines and payment options with the tax professional. In parallel, set up clean current-year books and an estimated-payment calendar.
records: IRS and state notices, transcripts and prior filed returns
Bank, credit-card, W-2 and 1099 records for affected years
Entity formation, election and payroll records
alternative: If records establish that a return was already filed correctly, remove it from the cleanup scope. If a balance is disputed, substantiate the correction before pursuing a payment arrangement. Relief eligibility depends on the actual facts; a large balance alone does not establish qualification for a settlement or penalty abatement.
deliverable: A prioritized filing and payment roadmap, followed by a current-year projection based on reconciled records. No refund, debt reduction or collection outcome is represented as achieved.
source_label: IRS: Filing Past Due Tax Returns

title: An Owner Models the Tax Cost of Cash at Closing and a Future Earnout
summary: Compare after-tax proceeds, income character and payment timing before the sale terms become fixed.
situation: An owner is negotiating a business sale with cash at closing, a later contingent payment and a possible consulting arrangement. The owner is also starting a new venture and would like to reinvest quickly. A large headline purchase price obscures how much cash can safely be committed after transaction costs and taxes.
decision: The deal documents must explain what each payment buys. Consideration for assets or ownership, payment for future services and financing interest can have different treatment. A closing date near year-end also makes payment timing relevant, but moving a signature date is not a complete tax plan.
rule: A business asset sale generally requires allocation among the assets sold. Installment treatment has exceptions, and depreciation recapture may be recognized in the sale year even when some proceeds arrive later. Contingent payments require transaction-specific analysis.
recommendation: Ask the transaction adviser, attorney and preparer to review the proposed terms together before signing. Model a base case, a reduced earnout and a delayed payment. Show transaction expenses, income character, state exposure and tax reserves beside cash receipts. Reserve funds before transferring closing proceeds into the new business.
records: Letter of intent, draft purchase agreement and payment schedule
Ownership basis, asset depreciation detail and transaction expense ledger
Consulting, employment, escrow and contingent-payment terms
alternative: If the agreement is already binding, focus on accurate reporting and funding rather than suggesting that the transaction can be rewritten after the fact. If a buyer offers a higher price for different terms, compare the after-tax and collection-risk outcomes instead of the gross prices alone.
deliverable: An after-tax proceeds schedule and a reserve policy for closing and subsequent payments. This illustration does not assert that an earnout is capital gain or that all deferred proceeds qualify for installment reporting.

title: A Storm-Damaged Rental Needs One Reconciled Loss and Rebuilding Schedule
summary: Coordinate casualty reporting, insurance proceeds and replacement assets before adding a new depreciation study.
situation: A rental owner repairs a property after severe storms and replaces damaged furnishings. Prior returns include casualty-related deductions, but the insurance claims settled across more than one year. The owner now wants a cost segregation study and worries that the preparer may have counted some costs twice.
decision: The next deduction cannot be evaluated in isolation. Each damaged component needs a history: prior basis, depreciation, damage, reimbursement and replacement. A contractor’s rebuilding invoice and an insurer’s payment may describe overlapping costs, while a prior return may already have adjusted the property’s basis.
rule: Casualty calculations take insurance and expected reimbursements into account. Business and personal portions must be distinguished. A loss deduction, reimbursement and replacement expenditure can each affect the subsequent tax analysis, so they need a coordinated reconciliation.
recommendation: Create a claim-by-claim timeline and reconcile it to the returns. Have the preparer review casualty treatment and basis adjustments before the study team uses the asset ledger. Track replacement furnishings and improvements separately from damaged assets, and document when the property became available again. Investigate discrepancies before concluding that an amendment is needed.
records: Insurance claims, adjuster reports and settlement correspondence
Prior casualty calculations and fixed-asset schedules
Repair and replacement invoices, photographs and service dates
alternative: If a claim remains open, identify assumptions that may change instead of treating an expected recovery as settled. If part of the property was personal-use, keep that allocation visible. A new study should not reproduce a deduction already reflected in an earlier loss or asset adjustment.
deliverable: A single reconciliation connecting claims, returns and replacement assets, followed by a supported study scope. No casualty amount, amended-return refund or accelerated deduction is claimed as a completed result.
source_label: IRS Publication 547: Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts
